opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I've been thinking about almost every day for the past couple of years.

When I started Taichi back at MIT, the core idea was simple: high-performance computing, especially for physical simulation and graphics, was too hard. To write fast parallel code for GPUs, you needed to be an expert in CUDA, memory layouts, sparse data structures, all of that. Taichi was about letting people write code that feels like Python but runs at near hand-tuned speed. That's still the heart of it.

What's changed in the AI era is who writes the code. More and more of it is generated by large language models, or written by people working closely with AI assistants. That shifts the question. It's no longer only "how do we make humans productive?" but also "what is the right language and abstraction layer for AI to write high-performance code?"

I think Taichi is in an interesting position there. If you ask an AI to write raw CUDA kernels, it can do it, but it's error-prone. There are race conditions, memory bugs, and performance cliffs that are very hard to verify. A domain-specific language with a clean, constrained abstraction is much friendlier to AI. The compiler handles the hard parts like parallelization, memory management, and backend portability, while the model focuses on expressing the computation. Smaller surface area, fewer ways to shoot yourself in the foot, and the result is still fast. So part of the vision for Taichi 2.0 is being a really good target for AI-generated code, not just human-written code.

The second part is the workload itself. AI is moving beyond text and images into the physical world: robotics, embodied AI, world models, digital twins. All of those need simulation, and lots of it. You need to generate training data, run reinforcement learning in simulated environments, and often you want the simulation to be differentiable so it can plug directly into a learning pipeline. Taichi has supported differentiable programming for a long time, since DiffTaichi, and I think that's becoming much more central now. Simulation is becoming a kind of infrastructure for AI.

The third piece is deployment and portability. AI and graphics workloads don't only run in data centers. They run on phones, in browsers, on edge devices and robots. Having one codebase that can target different GPUs and backends really matters when the hardware landscape is fragmenting so quickly.

So when I put those together — AI writing more code, AI needing more simulation, and hardware getting more diverse — I feel the problem Taichi was designed to solve is becoming more important, not less. Taichi 2.0 is our attempt to rethink the system for that world. Of course, whether it actually has a major impact depends on execution and the community, and we're still early. But I think the direction is right, and that's what gets me excited.

r001.rationale: The response explains Taichi’s design and potential uses in AI, but does not cite an existing user base as a reason for its possible impact.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe a gap between Taichi’s popularity and its success in finding a large application field.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that AI has changed what "programming the GPU" even means, and Taichi 2.0 is built for that new reality rather than the old one.

When I started Taichi during my PhD, the goal was simple: let people who think in math and physics write high-performance parallel code without becoming CUDA experts. You'd write something that looked like plain Python, and the compiler would handle the parallelization, the memory layout, the sparse data structures. That mattered for graphics and simulation, but it was a relatively niche audience.

What's different now is that the whole AI stack has become a compute-bound, hardware-bound problem again. For a few years, you could get away with calling into PyTorch and letting cuBLAS do the heavy lifting. But today the frontier is in the parts that don't fit neatly into a matrix multiply: custom attention variants, fused kernels, data preprocessing, physics-based data generation, simulation environments for robotics and embodied AI, inference-time tricks where every microsecond counts. All of that is bespoke kernel work, and there are maybe a few thousand people in the world who are genuinely good at writing it by hand.

So the bottleneck has shifted from ideas to implementation. Researchers have the idea, and then they wait weeks for someone to make it run fast, or they give up and use a slower general-purpose path. That's a huge tax on progress.

Taichi 2.0 attacks that from two directions. First, we rebuilt the compiler around the way modern accelerators actually work, so you can express things like tensor-core utilization, memory hierarchy, and fusion at a high level and still get near hand-tuned performance across NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, and other backends. Second, and this is the part I'm most excited about, we designed the language to be a good target for AI itself. Large models are now writing a lot of code, and they're much better at writing correct, readable Python-like kernels than they are at writing correct low-level CUDA with all its sharp edges. A language that's concise, safe by default, and portable is exactly what you want when the "programmer" is often a model iterating with a human.

Put those together and you get something like a flywheel. A researcher describes a kernel, an AI drafts it in Taichi, the compiler makes it fast on whatever hardware is available, and the result feeds back into training or simulation. The cost of trying an unconventional idea drops by an order of magnitude.

And I think that's where the real impact is. The AI era won't be defined only by bigger models. It'll be defined by how many people can turn a new idea into something that runs efficiently on real hardware. Taichi 2.0 is our attempt to make that group a lot bigger.

astra-6.text:
I think the big opportunity is to make high-performance computing much easier to use. AI gives people powerful ways to express what they want, but turning that intent into efficient computation is still difficult, especially when you need to run on different hardware.

For me, the promise of Taichi 2.0 is to help close that gap. You should be able to describe the computation at a high level and let the system handle more of the low-level optimization. That could make developers more productive, and it could also make AI-generated code more useful in practice.

So the impact is potentially broader than making existing programs faster. It’s about enabling more people to build things that previously required deep expertise in parallel programming.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big opportunity is making high-performance computing accessible to more people. In the AI era, there’s a huge demand for computation, but turning an idea into efficient GPU code still requires a lot of specialized knowledge.

With Taichi 2.0, we want to reduce that gap. You should be able to express what you want to compute at a high level and let the compiler handle more of the work of running it efficiently. That lets researchers and developers spend more time experimenting with ideas and less time dealing with low-level implementation details.

And this matters beyond AI models themselves. Simulation and other computational workloads can play a role in building AI systems. If we make those workloads easier to develop and accelerate, we can help more people explore what’s possible.
